---
title: "Design Philosophy"
---

IrisPipe is designed around one question: **what does it mean to re-run a pipeline that previously failed?**
Most pipeline tools treat re-execution as running the same config again from scratch.
IrisPipe treats it as three distinct operations — each with a different contract, different lineage, and different config source.

---

## Pipeline Data Model

Every pipeline is a strict hierarchy. Resources at each level have their own identity, persistence, and semantics.

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  W(["Workspace"]):::root --> S1["Stage 1"]
  W --> S2["Stage 2"]
  W --> S3["Stage 3"]

  subgraph "Pipeline"
    S1 --- J1["Job A"]
    S1 --- J2["Job B"]
    S2 --- J3["Job C"]
    S3 --- J4["Job D"]
    S3 --- J5["Job E"]
  end

  classDef root fill:#6366f1,color:#fff,stroke:none,rx:8
  classDef stage fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1,color:#3730a3
  classDef job fill:#f0fdf4,stroke:#16a34a,color:#15803d

  class S1,S2,S3 stage
  class J1,J2,J3,J4,J5 job
```

**Workspace** — scopes all resources. Resolved from `X-Iris-Workspace-Key` header; falls back to `default`.

**Folder** — explicit tree node, not a path-string convention. Supports rename, move, and recursive delete with preview.

**Pipeline** — uniquely identified by `(workspace, folder, pipelineName)`. Identity is not tied to file path.

**Stage** — sequential execution barrier. All stages must complete in order. Stages are a first-class concept in both config and runtime APIs.

**Job** — parallel unit within a stage. Jobs in the same stage run concurrently via Spring Batch. Each job owns its own `source → destination` JDBC connection pair.

**Step** — atomic SQL operation within a job. Steps execute sequentially. Types: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `UPSERT`, `DELETE`, `EXECUTE`.

---

## Job Config Model

Each job within a stage declares its own data movement contract. Below is the full shape of a job and its steps.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
  J["Job\n──────\nstage_name\nstage_sequence_order\njob_name\natomic_level\nwatermark_column\nwatermark_type"]

  J --> SRC["Source\n──────────\nconnection_id (FK)\nor inline url/driver\ncredentials"]

  J --> DST["Destination\n──────────\nconnection_id (FK)\nor inline url/driver\ncredentials"]

  J --> E1["Step 1\n─────────────\nexecution_type\nsource_sql\ndestination_table"]
  J --> E2["Step 2\n─────────────\nexecution_type\ndestination_table"]
  J --> E3["Step N ..."]

  style J fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1
  style SRC fill:#f0fdf4,stroke:#16a34a
  style DST fill:#fff7ed,stroke:#f59e0b
  style E1 fill:#fdf2f8,stroke:#a855f7
  style E2 fill:#fdf2f8,stroke:#a855f7
  style E3 fill:#fdf2f8,stroke:#a855f7
```

**Execution types** — controls how each step writes to the destination:

| Type | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `INSERT` | `INSERT INTO dest SELECT ...` |
| `UPDATE` | `UPDATE dest SET ... WHERE ...` |
| `UPSERT` | Merge — insert or update on conflict |
| `DELETE` | `DELETE FROM dest WHERE ...` |
| `EXECUTE` | Arbitrary SQL (DDL, stored procedure) |

Steps within a job execute **sequentially** in their declared order.

---

## Connection Model

A job's source and destination can be configured in two ways:

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  J["Job"]

  J -- "named" --> C["iris_connection\n──────────\nconnection_name\ndriver\nurl\ncredentials"]

  J -- "inline" --> I["Inline config\n──────────\ndriver\nurl\nusername / password\n(stored on job row)"]

  style C fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1
  style I fill:#fff7ed,stroke:#f59e0b
```

**Named connections** (`iris_connection` library) are reusable across jobs. A change to the named connection propagates to all jobs referencing it — but only for future `execute` calls. Existing run snapshots are unaffected.

**Inline connections** embed credentials directly on the job config. They are convenient for one-off jobs but cannot be updated globally.

---

## Stage Barrier + Parallel Execution

The key scheduling primitive is the **stage barrier**:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  subgraph "Stage 1 — parallel"
    direction TB
    J1["Job A\n(extract orders)"]
    J2["Job B\n(extract users)"]
    J3["Job C\n(extract products)"]
  end

  subgraph "Stage 2 — parallel"
    direction TB
    J4["Job D\n(transform)"]
  end

  subgraph "Stage 3 — parallel"
    direction TB
    J5["Job E\n(load warehouse)"]
    J6["Job F\n(load reporting)"]
  end

  Stage1 -- "barrier\n(all must COMPLETE)" --> Stage2
  Stage2 -- "barrier\n(all must COMPLETE)" --> Stage3
```

- Jobs within a stage are launched concurrently via Spring Batch `JobLauncher`
- The engine waits at each barrier until **all** jobs in that stage reach a terminal state
- If **any** job fails at a barrier, all subsequent stages are projected as `NOT_RUN`
- If a job is stopped, its stage barrier also fails, and future stages become `NOT_RUN`

---

## Three Execution Verbs

The core design decision: **re-execution is not one thing**. IrisPipe provides three distinct operations with different contracts:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  E(["execute"]):::blue --> E1["reads live config"]
  E --> E2["new PipelineRun"]
  E --> E3["Stage 1 →"]

  R(["resume"]):::green --> R1["reads same snapshot"]
  R --> R2["new Attempt\nin same Run"]
  R --> R3["resume stage →"]

  RR(["rerun"]):::amber --> RR1["reads same snapshot"]
  RR --> RR2["new PipelineRun"]
  RR --> RR3["Stage 1 →"]

  classDef blue fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1,color:#3730a3
  classDef green fill:#f0fdf4,stroke:#16a34a,color:#15803d
  classDef amber fill:#fff7ed,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#92400e
```

**Resume** detail — how the engine picks up where it left off:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A["resume(runId)"] --> B["Load snapshot\n(same run)"]
  B --> C["Find first incomplete stage"]
  C --> D["Mark upstream jobs SKIPPED"]
  D --> E["Launch from that stage"]

  style A fill:#f0fdf4,stroke:#16a34a
```

### `execute` — Fresh run from live config

Creates a **new logical run**. This is the only operation that reads the current stored pipeline config.
At execute time, a **config snapshot** is persisted — the run is insulated from all future config edits.

### `resume` — Continue a failed run

Creates a **new execution attempt** within the same logical run. The run identity, lineage, and snapshot are all preserved.

Resume logic:
1. Load the persisted snapshot for this run
2. Find the first stage containing `FAILED`, `STOPPED`, or `NOT_RUN` jobs
3. Mark all jobs in successfully completed stages as `SKIPPED`
4. Relaunch only from the resume stage

For `atomicLevel = JOB` jobs: replay the failed job as a fresh Spring Batch job instance.

For `atomicLevel = CHUNK` jobs: restart the failed Spring Batch job instance with stable parameters — execution resumes at the last committed chunk, not from the start of the job.

### `rerun` — Replay from scratch using original config

Creates a **new logical run** from the source run's snapshot. Useful when you want a clean audit record (fresh row counts, new run ID) while preserving the exact config version that was originally used.

### Decision table

| Scenario | Correct verb |
|---|---|
| Fixed a bug in the SQL — want a fresh run with new config | `execute` |
| Stage 2 failed, Stage 1 succeeded — replay only Stage 2 | `resume` |
| Config was modified after execute — want to retry with original config | `resume` |
| Want a clean historical record using the same original config | `rerun` |
| Scheduled daily run | `execute` |

---

## Snapshot Isolation

The snapshot mechanism is the enabling primitive for safe resume and rerun:

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
  actor User
  participant Engine
  participant DB as Config DB
  participant Snap as Snapshot Store

  User->>Engine: execute(pipelineId)
  Engine->>DB: read live config
  DB-->>Engine: SyncJobDefinition[]
  Engine->>Snap: persist snapshot JSON
  Note over Snap: ← config frozen here
  Engine-->>User: PipelineRun created

  Note over DB: User edits config (rename job, change SQL)

  User->>Engine: resume(runId)
  Engine->>Snap: load snapshot (same run)
  Note over Snap: live config never read
  Engine-->>User: Resume attempt launched
```

Snapshot payload stores:
- All `SyncJobDefinition[]` with stage names and ordering
- Materialized Spring Batch job execution names (stable across attempts)
- `pipeline_content_hash` for integrity verification
- `snapshot_schema_version` for future migration

---

## Stop Semantics

Stop is **cooperative**, not force-kill:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A["stop(runId)"] --> B{"Validate execution state"}
  B -- "STARTING / STARTED / STOPPING" --> C["Project execution → STOPPING"]
  B -- "other state" --> Z["Reject: not stoppable"]

  C --> D["Call JobOperator.stop()\nfor each in-flight Spring Batch job"]
  D --> E["Spring Batch sets stop signal\non running step"]
  E --> F["Step checks stop signal\nat chunk boundary"]
  F --> G["CustomJobListener\nonJobExecutionStopped"]
  G --> H["PipelineRunLifecycleService\nproject STOPPED"]
  H --> I["Future stages → NOT_RUN"]

  style C fill:#fff7ed,stroke:#f59e0b
  style H fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1
```

**Settlement guard**: Because Spring Batch metadata can still be finalizing after IrisPipe has already projected `STOPPED`, the `resume` path waits briefly before launching a new attempt. This prevents a race between a settling stopped execution and a new resume attempt reading stale Batch state.

---

## AtomicLevel: Two Resume Strategies

Each job declares its `atomicLevel`, which controls what "resume" means at the job level:

| `atomicLevel` | Resume behavior | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| `JOB` | Replay the whole job as a new Batch job instance | Simple jobs, idempotent SQL |
| `CHUNK` | Restart the same Batch job instance at the last commit point | Large table reads where replaying from the start is expensive |

`JOB` is the default. `CHUNK` requires that the Spring Batch job instance parameters produce a stable identity across resume attempts — IrisPipe materializes these from the snapshot.

---

## Runtime Lineage Model

A single pipeline can have many runs. A single run can have many execution attempts.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  Run["PipelineRun\n(logical run)"]
  Snap["RunSnapshot\n(immutable config)"]
  RunJob["RunJob ×N\n← latest projection"]
  Exec1["Execution #1\nINITIAL · FAILED"]
  Exec2["Execution #2\nRESUME · COMPLETED"]
  EJ1["ExecJob ×N\n(per attempt)"]
  EJ2["ExecJob ×N\n(per attempt)"]

  Run --> Snap
  Run --> RunJob
  Run --> Exec1
  Run --> Exec2
  Exec1 --> EJ1
  Exec2 --> EJ2

  style Snap fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#ca8a04
  style RunJob fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1
  style Exec1 fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444
  style Exec2 fill:#f0fdf4,stroke:#16a34a
```

Two read paths coexist in the same schema:

- **`PipelineRun` + `PipelineRunJob`** — latest projection, used for cheap list and summary APIs
- **`PipelineRunExecution` + `PipelineRunExecutionJob`** — full attempt history, used for run detail and audit

---

## Design Principles

### 1. Workspace-scoped, not global

The engine resolves workspace from request scope. Desktop mode works through the `default` fallback without ever setting the header.

### 2. JSON CRUD as the primary contract

Config management is body-driven first, file import second. Import is an adapter, not the identity model.

### 3. Facade + Collaborator, not monolithic services

Services are split into application-boundary facades and narrow collaborators. This reduces coupling between read and write paths and keeps unit-testable slices small.

### 4. Listener-driven runtime truth

Trigger APIs create rows and launch work. They do not own final status. Listeners report actual Batch transitions. The lifecycle service projects truth back into runtime rows.

### 5. Observability from lifecycle, not from controllers

Metrics are published by `PipelineMetricsPublisher` in response to lifecycle events — not from controller logic. Meter code never appears in DTOs or controllers.

### 6. k6 as architectural guardrail

The 10-suite k6 regression harness runs against the real backend on every push. This allows internal refactoring with confidence: change the package structure, restructure service boundaries, split collaborators — the k6 suite will catch any public behavioral regression.
